# Question 8

# What R cycling did to shirt is that it kept repeating the process because z has (length 6) so it kept repeating until it reached the 6th element and stop there. That's why the result was (2 2 4 4 6 6) it kept adding 1 and 0 up until reaches the end element.

# Question 9
```{r}
ztest <- c(1, 0, 1)
zshort <- c(1, 0)

sumTest <- ztest + zshort
sumTest
```
# Yes, it works cleanly without showing any warnings.

```{r}
ztest2 <- c(1, 0, 1, 1)
zshort2 <- c(1, 0)

sumTest2 <- ztest2 + zshort2
sumTest2
```
# R recycles silently when the length of the longer vector is an exact integer multiple of the shorter vector's length.

# Question 11

# lists is a heterogenous which means it holds many data types, this needs a distinction because list elements can contain a whole data structure. Meanwhile for Vector, this can only hold elements of a single data type. 

Part E
```{r}
inventory <- list( item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
                   price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
                   in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))

inventory[["item"]][inventory$in_stock]
```

```{r}
inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$price <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)
```

# Question 12

# R first evaluates inventory[[item]] and inventory[[in_stock]] separately, both parallel vectors are then extracted. Position 1: TRUE Keep = "Notebook"   Position 2: TRUE = Keep "Pen"   Position 3: FALSE = Drop "Eraser" . It worked because logical indexing relies on positional alignment. 

# Question 13

# This creates a problem for example Accidental Misalignement, Mismatch. If you sort item_prices to see the cheapest items first, item_names and item_stock won't automatically sort with it. The prices end up attached to the wrong products, completely messing up the dataset. I support using a list instead. It keeps all related information bundled in one place so that when you filter, sort, or update something.

# Conclusion

# List holds many data types meanwhile vector can only hold a single data type. Their differences varies the way you would use it, if you want a standard and direct way to navigate through a singular data set use a vector and if the dataset is larger and more complex and offer to use more data types then use lists. I would use lists when im given a task with the use of multiple data types, and if im only dealing with singular data type I would rather choose the vector for easier navigation.
